title: The five virtues as medicine
tomorrow: Bebe goes home Sunday. which thief is quieter in Simran now?

cards: Simran is at the kitchen table watching Bebe do her ankle exercises: heel up, heel down, the way the therapist's sheet on the fridge says, three times a day. Simran asks: so, five thieves, right?
Lust, anger, greed, attachment, pride. Is there a medicine for each one, or do you just fight them forever? Bebe keeps lifting her heel.
Bebe has done these every day since the boot came off, even the days she grumbled. She nods at the fridge and says: look.

teach.b: There is a medicine, and Sikh teachers name it in five virtues: sat, truth; santokh, contentment; daya, compassion; nimrata, humility; and pyaar, love.

Teachers pair them with the thieves in different ways, but some pairings are plain: compassion against anger, contentment against greed, humility against pride. The idea runs straight back to Gurbani.
In Asa di Var, on ang 466, the Guru says, in paraphrase: ego is a long illness, and its medicine is within it too.
And on ang 62, Guru Nanak says truth is higher than everything, and higher still is truthful living. Living, not knowing.
A virtue isn't a fact we learn about ourselves; it's something we do, on a Tuesday, when no one is checking. Here's what Bebe's fridge adds. A medicine isn't a speech; it's a dose.
Small, daily, a little boring. Nobody heals an ankle by thinking hard about ankles, or by doing a month of exercises in one afternoon. You lift the heel today, and again tomorrow.
So with the virtues: one honest sentence, one patient pause, one thing put back on the shelf.
Here's the line to repeat tonight: the virtue is the dose, not the diagnosis.
Simran takes a pen and writes under the therapy sheet: one virtue a day. Bebe reads it, puts on her glasses, reads it again, and says: good. You do yours, I'll do mine.
Then she lifts her heel one more time than the sheet asks.

how: Sikh teachers commonly set five virtues (sat, santokh, daya, nimrata, pyaar) against the five thieves, and Gurbani speaks of ego as an illness with a cure; the virtues are practiced in daily life, not only in prayer.

games.q: what does “the five virtues as medicine” mean?
o: five promises made at a Sikh wedding day
five virtues taken as small daily cures
five prayers said to drive out the thieves

p: ego is an illness; the cure is within

s: knowing the five virtues by name is most of the cure
ang 62: higher still is truthful living. the virtue is the dose, not the diagnosis.
Gurbani describes ego as an illness whose medicine is within it
the virtues work best as one big change, made all at once
like Bebe's heel lifts: small, daily, a little boring.

games.q: you've noticed you keep cutting people off in meetings. you've named the thief: pride. what fits today's idea of medicine?
o: a small daily dose: let one person finish first, each day.
a long, honest reflection on where your pride comes from.
a promise to stay silent in meetings from now on.
games.why: the virtue is the dose, not the diagnosis: humility, taken small and daily, the way Bebe lifts her heel.

practice: Choose one of the five: truth, contentment, compassion, humility or love.
Picture one moment later today when you'll need it, and the small dose you could take: one honest sentence, one pause before answering, one thing left on the shelf. Hold that picture, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: The five virtues as medicine. Truth, contentment, compassion, humility and love, taken in small daily doses.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: daaroo, medicine; on ang 466, ego is a long illness and its daaroo is within it.

carryVoice: The medicine: small doses, every day, like heel lifts on a sheet by the fridge. See you then.
